q: Trace how Melon de Bourgogne came to the Pays Nantais and why it stayed.
accept: gouais blanc x pinot brought west for the dutch distilling trade and replanted after the 1709 frost
burgundian grape replanted after the great frost of 1709
dutch brandy trade then the 1709 frost made it universal
cold hardy and early ripening so it survived the frost
ans: It is a Burgundian grape — a Gouais Blanc × Pinot crossing, and so a full sibling of Chardonnay, Aligoté and Gamay — pushed out of Burgundy by ducal edict in the sixteenth century. It moved west because the Dutch, who controlled the Atlantic trade out of Nantes, wanted thin, neutral, high-acid wine to distill into brandy, and Melon obliged. The catastrophic winter of 1708–09 froze the Nantais vineyard to death, and the cold-hardy, early-ripening Melon was replanted almost to the exclusion of everything else. It stayed because it ripens before the Atlantic autumn breaks, resists winter cold, and — the modern discovery — takes extended lees ageing better than its neutrality suggests, which is the whole argument of the crus communaux.
exp: Melon's history is entirely economic and climatic, never qualitative, which is why the region spent centuries being underrated. Being able to say that out loud — and then pivot to Clisson and Gorges as the correction — is the persuasive shape of the answer.

accept: both chenin vouvray north bank larger montlouis between the loire and cher
montlouis split from vouvray in 1938 sandier and more radical
vouvray larger and sweeter montlouis drier and ancestral method
montlouis smaller warmer soils earlier ripening
ans: Both are one hundred per cent Chenin Blanc on tuffeau, and both run the full ladder from sec to moelleux plus pétillant and mousseux. Vouvray lies on the north bank of the Loire and is roughly five times the size, with deeper clay-with-flint perruches and limestone-rich aubuis over the tuffeau, colder sites, later ripening and the greater sweet-wine reputation — Huet and Foreau are its monuments. Montlouis occupies the plateau between the Loire and the Cher, on sandier, warmer, faster-draining soils that ripen earlier and lend themselves to dry wine and sparkling. It only separated from Vouvray in 1938, having been sold as Vouvray before, and took the name Montlouis-sur-Loire in 2002. It has since been by far the more daring appellation: Chidaine, Blot and their generation legislated pétillant originel, the ancestral method, into existence in 2007, and Montlouis is now the centre of the region's dry-Chenin avant-garde.
exp: The comparison rewards structure: same grape, same rock, different river position, different soil depth, different regulatory temperament. The last point is the interesting one — Montlouis outran its famous neighbour by writing new law rather than defending old.

q: Set out the Anjou sweet-Chenin appellations in ascending order of concentration, and name the two that lie outside the Layon valley.
accept: layon then chaume premier cru then bonnezeaux and quarts de chaume with aubance and anjou coteaux de la loire outside
coteaux de l'aubance and anjou coteaux de la loire lie outside the layon
quarts de chaume grand cru at the top bonnezeaux beside it
chaume premier cru sits above coteaux du layon
ans: Ascending: Coteaux du Layon, with its named villages such as Rablay, Beaulieu, Saint-Aubin and Saint-Lambert; then Coteaux du Layon Premier Cru Chaume, which demands successive hand-picked tries and a far higher residual sugar; then the two enclaves that stand alone — Bonnezeaux, on the three hills above Thouarcé, and Quarts de Chaume, promoted in 2011 to the Loire's only Grand Cru, with the region's highest must weight requirement at 298 g/L and its lowest yields. Outside the Layon valley altogether: Coteaux de l'Aubance, on the little Aubance river between the Layon and Angers, and Anjou-Coteaux de la Loire, on the Loire itself around and above Savennières. All are Chenin, all on Armorican schist, and all depend on autumn mist off small rivers — the same mechanism as the Ciron at Sauternes, at a smaller scale.
exp: The hierarchy is a ladder of required concentration and falling yield, and the two outliers are what catch candidates who memorised only the Layon. Coteaux de l'Aubance in particular is a value hunting-ground worth naming on a floor.

q: Explain the Loire's place in the natural-wine movement and the labelling consequence that follows from it.
accept: growers declassify to vin de france after failing the agrement for typicity
puzelat angeli mosse cousin and vin de france labels
rejection on typicity means the appellation cannot be named on the label
the loire is the heartland and the wines end up as vin de france
ans: The Loire is the movement's French heartland alongside Beaujolais: Thierry Puzelat at Clos du Tue-Bœuf in Touraine, Mark Angeli at La Ferme de la Sansonnière, René and Agnès Mosse, Olivier Cousin, Richard Leroy in Anjou, Sébastien Riffault in Sancerre, and the annual Dive Bouteille tasting in the Saumur caves as its gathering point. The conditions are favourable: cheap land, small holdings, a tradition of polyculture, and varieties — Chenin, Cabernet Franc, Pineau d'Aunis, Grolleau — that tolerate low-intervention handling. The consequence is regulatory. Wines with oxidative, volatile or cloudy profiles routinely fail the agrément tasting for typicity, so growers declassify to Vin de France, which bars any mention of appellation or region; vintage and variety may still be shown, but only where the producer is certified for it. A great deal of the Loire's most interesting wine therefore leaves the region geographically anonymous, identifiable only by producer and cuvée name — and some growers now declassify pre-emptively, out of principle rather than rejection.
exp: This is a law-and-culture question, and the payoff is practical: if you cannot read a region off the label you must be able to read the producer. Note the precise scope of the demotion — Vin de France strips the geography, not the vintage, which a certified producer may still print. It also sets up the honest counter-argument about faults versus style, which a good oral answer should acknowledge rather than dodge.

q: What is 'Breton', where does the name come from, and what is Cabernet Franc's place in the family tree?
accept: breton is cabernet franc named for abbe breton parent of cabernet sauvignon and merlot
abbe breton richelieu's steward planted it in chinon and bourgueil
cabernet franc is the parent of cabernet sauvignon with sauvignon blanc and of merlot
called breton in the loire and it is bordeaux's ancestor
ans: Breton is the Loire's local name for Cabernet Franc. It commemorates the Abbé Breton, steward to Cardinal Richelieu, who propagated the vine through Chinon and Bourgueil in the seventeenth century — though Rabelais had already praised the wine of Chinon a century before that. The DNA matters more than the folklore: Cabernet Franc crossed with Sauvignon Blanc produced Cabernet Sauvignon, and crossed with Magdeleine Noire des Charentes produced Merlot; it is also a parent of Carmenère. In other words the Loire's grape is the ancestor of Bordeaux's, not a poor relation of them — the argument you make when someone calls Chinon a lesser claret.
exp: Orals reward the answer that turns a nomenclature question into an argument. The parentage is also examinable on its own: know both crossings and the fact that Cabernet Franc's home ground is the Loire and the Basque country, not the Médoc.
